title: National Coalition Launched to Protect Human Rights Defenders in DRC

title_en: National Coalition Launched to Protect Human Rights Defenders in DRC
excerpt_en: Kinshasa, May 1, 2026---A new national coalition aimed at strengthening the protection of human rights defenders has been launched in the Democratic Republic of Congo, bringing together civil society actors, organizations, and institutional stakeholders under a coordinated framework.
body_en:
Kinshasa, May 1, 2026---A new national coalition aimed at strengthening the protection of human rights defenders has been launched in the Democratic Republic of Congo, bringing together civil society actors, organizations, and institutional stakeholders under a coordinated framework.

The initiative, unveiled in Kinshasa, follows a three-day workshop that gathered human rights defenders, organization leaders, and authorities to address challenges related to the promotion and protection of fundamental rights. The coalition seeks to improve coordination, enhance information sharing, and reinforce collective responses to threats faced by civil society actors.

Structured around key priorities, the platform focuses on the protection of defenders, capacity building, and joint advocacy. It aims to provide both preventive and active protection mechanisms, while supporting defenders through training in areas such as digital security, physical safety, and documentation of human rights violations.

The creation of the coalition marks a significant step in a process that has spanned nearly two decades, during which previous attempts at establishing a unified structure had struggled to reach consensus. With this development, the DRC joins a broader continental network of similar coalitions established across Africa.

The launch comes despite recent legislative progress, including the adoption of a law in 2023 establishing a legal framework for the protection and responsibilities of human rights defenders. However, challenges persist, particularly in conflict-affected regions in the east of the country, where insecurity and political tensions continue to expose activists to risks.

Civil society representatives emphasized the importance of the coalition as a tool to safeguard civic space and strengthen solidarity among defenders. The event also featured the presentation of a report highlighting the current situation of human rights defenders, described as a call for urgent action to ensure safer working conditions.

Participants paid tribute to defenders who lost their lives in the line of duty, underscoring the importance of preserving their memory while continuing efforts to protect those still at risk.

Speakers at the event stressed the need for unity and collaboration, noting that isolated defenders are more vulnerable to threats, while collective action enhances their ability to engage effectively with institutions. Calls were also made to ensure greater inclusion of marginalized groups, including Indigenous defenders, within the coalition.

body_en:
KINSHASA, May 9, 2026 - The Alliance of Democratic Forces of Congo (AFDC), led by Senator Modeste Bahati, has condemned the arrest of its National Vice-President, Hilaire Kasusa Kikobya, along with four of his colleagues at Ngobila Beach in Kinshasa.

According to information released by the party, Hilaire Kasusa Kikobya, who also serves as Chairman of the Board of Directors of INERA, was returning from an official mission to Brazzaville when he was apprehended.

Among those arrested were lawyer Jean-Claude Phukuta Kuala, who had come to welcome him, as well as Yvon Yanga and Valery Ilunga. The group was reportedly transferred to the premises of DEMIAP, the military intelligence service.

The circumstances and reasons surrounding the arrests remain unclear. The AFDC-A has called for the immediate release of the detained officials, insisting that they have no dispute with any authority.

title_en: Belgium’s Conviction for Colonial-Era Crimes in Congo Becomes Final After Appeal Rejected
excerpt_en: Brussels, May 22, 2026 - Belgium has been definitively condemned for crimes against humanity committed during the colonial era in the former Belgian Congo, following the rejection of an appeal by the country’s Court of Cassation.
body_en:
Brussels, May 22, 2026 - Belgium has been definitively condemned for crimes against humanity committed during the colonial era in the former Belgian Congo, following the rejection of an appeal by the country’s Court of Cassation.

The ruling confirms a 2024 decision holding the Belgian state responsible for acts of racial segregation and the forced removal of mixed-race children during the colonial administration of what is now the Democratic Republic of Congo.

With the appeal rejected, the judgment has now become final, obliging Belgium to compensate victims affected by the colonial-era policies.

The case was brought by five mixed-race women born between 1948 and 1952 who were separated from their Congolese mothers as children and placed in religious institutions under the Belgian colonial system.

The plaintiffs - Marie-Josée Loshi, Noëlle Verbeken, Léa Tavares Mujinga, Simone Ngalula, and Monique Bintu Bingi - argued that they were stripped of their identities and family ties through a system designed to enforce racial segregation during the colonial period.

According to the court, the removals formed part of a broader institutional policy implemented by Belgian colonial authorities.

During the proceedings, the women described being separated from their families, deprived of their names and identities, and abandoned following Congo’s independence in 1960.

“The Belgian state uprooted us, separated us from our families, stole our names, our identities, and our human rights,” Léa Tavares Mujinga stated during the hearings.

title: Nine Inmates Granted Parole at Overcrowded Kangbayi Prison in Beni
excerpt: Beni, North Kivu - May 29, 2026 - Nine convicted inmates have been granted conditional release from Kangbayi Central Prison in Beni, in a supervised parole operation led by provincial authorities.
title_en: Nine Inmates Granted Parole at Overcrowded Kangbayi Prison in Beni
excerpt_en: Beni, North Kivu - May 29, 2026 - Nine convicted inmates have been granted conditional release from Kangbayi Central Prison in Beni, in a supervised parole operation led by provincial authorities.
body_en:
Beni, North Kivu - May 29, 2026 - Nine convicted inmates have been granted conditional release from Kangbayi Central Prison in Beni, in a supervised parole operation led by provincial authorities.

The procedure was overseen by the Deputy Governor of North Kivu, Commissioner Louis Segond Karawa, who met with judicial and prison officials before presiding over the formal roll call of beneficiaries selected for release.

According to the Prosecutor General at the North Kivu Court of Appeal, Thierry Tshiswaka Kabeya, the released inmates met legal eligibility criteria, including having served a minimum portion of their sentences, demonstrating good conduct, and not being involved in serious offenses such as violent crimes, sexual violence, insurrection, or criminal conspiracy.

The conditional release was carried out under a ministerial decree governing parole measures, with official release documents handed over to the beneficiaries on behalf of the Ministry of Justice.

Authorities urged the released individuals to reintegrate responsibly and avoid returning to criminal activity. In response, the beneficiaries reportedly pledged to respect the law and contribute positively to society.

The parole operation comes amid persistent concerns over severe overcrowding at Kangbayi Central Prison, which was originally designed for 200 inmates but currently holds more than 1,300 detainees-over six times its intended capacity.

Human rights and civil society organizations have repeatedly warned about deteriorating conditions inside the facility, including reported food shortages affecting inmates and multiple deaths recorded earlier in the year. These conditions continue to raise broader concerns about prison management and detainee welfare in the province.

title: La RDC saisit la CIJ contre le Rwanda pour violations du droit international
excerpt: THE HAGUE, June 26, 2026 - The Democratic Republic of the Congo has formally instituted proceedings against Rwanda before the International Court of Justice (ICJ), accusing its neighbor of committing serious violations of international law linked to the long-running conflict in eastern DRC.
title_en: DRC Files Case Against Rwanda at International Court of Justice Over Alleged International Law Violations
excerpt_en: THE HAGUE, June 26, 2026 - The Democratic Republic of the Congo has formally instituted proceedings against Rwanda before the International Court of Justice (ICJ), accusing its neighbor of committing serious violations of international law linked to the long-running conflict in eastern DRC.
body_en:
THE HAGUE, June 26, 2026 - The Democratic Republic of the Congo has formally instituted proceedings against Rwanda before the International Court of Justice (ICJ), accusing its neighbor of committing serious violations of international law linked to the long-running conflict in eastern DRC.

The application was filed in The Hague by Minister of State and Minister of Justice Guillaume Ngefa, marking a new phase in the dispute between the two countries after years of military, diplomatic and political tensions.

According to the Congolese government, the case seeks a ruling that Rwanda bears international responsibility for alleged violations of several international treaties, including the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide (1948), the International Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Racial Discrimination (1965), the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women (1979) and the Convention against Torture (1984).

Kinshasa argues that civilians in eastern DRC have endured more than three decades of massacres, extrajudicial killings, torture, sexual violence, forced displacement and discrimination, which it attributes to the actions of Rwanda and armed groups allegedly supported or controlled by Kigali.

The Congolese government further alleges that, following the 1994 Rwandan genocide, Rwandan armed forces and allied rebel movements conducted unlawful military operations on Congolese territory, targeting refugee camps, villages and urban centers, resulting in widespread civilian casualties and displacement.

According to the application, these alleged violations continued during the First and Second Congo Wars and subsequent conflicts through the activities of armed groups including the Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo (AFDL), the Congolese Rally for Democracy (RCD), the National Congress for the Defence of the People (CNDP), and the AFC/M23 movement.

The DRC is asking the Court to declare Rwanda internationally responsible, order the cessation of the alleged wrongful acts, require guarantees of non-repetition and award full reparations to the Congolese state and victims in accordance with international law.

The government said the legal action reflects its commitment to resolving disputes through peaceful means and to seeking accountability through international law while pursuing justice for victims of the conflict.

title: Deux soldats condamnés à mort pour le meurtre d'une infirmière au Haut-Uele
excerpt: ISIRO, June 22, 2026 - A military court in Isiro has sentenced two soldiers of the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (FARDC) to death for the murder of a nurse in Mungbere, Watsa Territory, Haut-Uele Province.
title_en: Two Soldiers Sentenced to Death for Killing Nurse in Haut-Uele
excerpt_en: ISIRO, June 22, 2026 - A military court in Isiro has sentenced two soldiers of the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (FARDC) to death for the murder of a nurse in Mungbere, Watsa Territory, Haut-Uele Province.
body_en:
ISIRO, June 22, 2026 - A military court in Isiro has sentenced two soldiers of the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (FARDC) to death for the murder of a nurse in Mungbere, Watsa Territory, Haut-Uele Province.

The convictions were handed down during summary proceedings after the court found the two soldiers guilty of criminal conspiracy, disobeying military orders and murder.

The incident occurred on June 7, when a warrant officer and a private, who had been deployed to Watsa as part of military operations against the Allied Democratic Forces (ADF), allegedly killed a nurse and wounded a civilian in Mungbere.

In addition to the death sentence, the private was sentenced to five years of penal servitude for aggravated assault and battery. The court also ordered him to pay the victim's family the equivalent of US$50,000 in damages.

Two other soldiers were each sentenced to three years of penal servitude for violating military regulations. The court granted them mitigating circumstances based on their young age.

A fifth soldier was acquitted after the court found insufficient evidence to establish his involvement in the case.

body_en:
KINSHASA, June 25, 2026 - Exiled opposition figure André Claudel Lubaya has denounced the continued detention of senior officials of the People's Party for Reconstruction and Democracy (PPRD), saying their prolonged incarceration without trial undermines the rule of law and raises serious concerns about respect for fundamental rights in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

In an opinion piece, Lubaya criticized what he described as the "deafening political and judicial silence" surrounding the cases of Aubin Minaku, Emmanuel Ramazani Shadary and Dunia Kilanga, senior members of former President Joseph Kabila's party who have been detained since late 2025 and early 2026.

More than seven months after their arrests, Lubaya questioned the legal basis for their continued detention, asking what charges had been brought against them, what investigative steps had been taken and why judicial proceedings had not advanced.

"On these fundamental questions, the persistent silence of the proceedings inevitably fuels doubts," he wrote.

Lubaya also alleged that the detainees had been transferred repeatedly between undisclosed detention facilities without their families or legal representatives being informed of their whereabouts.

He argued that such practices violate the basic principles of the rule of law and deprive detainees of judicial oversight and access to legal counsel.

"When a state deprives citizens of their freedom, removes them from their families, their lawyers and the oversight of judges, it is not merely taking away their liberty-it is making them disappear from the realm of the law," Lubaya said. "A democracy cannot tolerate citizens being relegated to the blind spots of justice."

The opposition figure also criticized what he described as the limited reaction of human rights organizations and the Democratic Republic of the Congo's international partners to the continued detention of opposition politicians.

title_en: Delly Sesanga Says DGM Seized Passport, Ordered Him to Appear Before Court of Cassation
excerpt_en: KINSHASA, June 28, 2026 - Opposition leader Delly Sesanga says the General Directorate of Migration (DGM) confiscated his passport and prevented him from traveling to Europe for medical treatment, informing him only that he was required to appear before the Court of Cassation.
body_en:
KINSHASA, June 28, 2026 - Opposition leader Delly Sesanga says the General Directorate of Migration (DGM) confiscated his passport and prevented him from traveling to Europe for medical treatment, informing him only that he was required to appear before the Court of Cassation.

The president of the Envol party said he was denied boarding at Kinshasa's international airport after immigration officials seized his passport.

"They took my passport and refused me boarding," Sesanga said, adding that no formal explanation was provided for the measure.

According to Sesanga, immigration officials told him only that he was expected to appear before the Court of Cassation but did not present any official summons or specify the legal basis for the order.

"I was never notified of anything," he said.

Sesanga stated that he had planned to travel to Europe for medical treatment related to injuries he said he sustained during the June 12 demonstration. He claimed to be suffering from ten serious injuries requiring specialized care.

The opposition leader described the confiscation of his passport as an arbitrary restriction on his constitutional right to freedom of movement.

"This is an act of violence against my freedom of movement, guaranteed by the Constitution," he said, adding that he intended to challenge the measure through legal means.

body_en:

In a statement, the military prosecution office said that ongoing investigations have, at this stage, uncovered what it described as “solid evidence” indicating the involvement of certain military personnel, including both active-duty and discharged soldiers, in the planning, coordination, and execution of the attacks.

The statement also alleges the involvement of political figures, including Dr. Oumar Mariko, in connection with the case, alongside individuals identified as suspected accomplices within and outside the armed forces.

Among those named in the investigation is Alassane Diallo, also known as Abedi, a discharged soldier who reportedly died during the clashes in Kati. Other individuals listed as suspected co-perpetrators include Sergeant Diakaridia Sodio, Warrant Officer Moussa Diane, Chief Warrant Officer Mamadou Keita, all active-duty personnel, as well as retired soldier Soïba Diarra.

Authorities confirmed that initial arrests have already been carried out, while further suspects are actively being sought as part of the ongoing operation.

The military prosecutor praised the work of investigative and security units, stating that the inquiry will continue in strict accordance with legal procedures. Officials added that further updates will be communicated to the public as the investigation progresses.

body_en:
Paris, May 7, 2026 - The Paris Court of Appeal has ordered the continuation of investigations into Agathe Kanziga, widow of former Rwandan President Juvénal Habyarimana, over allegations linked to the 1994 Genocide against the Tutsi and its preparation.

The ruling, issued on May 6, 2026, overturns a previous decision made by an investigating judge in August 2025, which had concluded that there was insufficient evidence to establish Kanziga’s involvement in the genocide. At the time, the judge had indicated that she appeared more affected by the assassination of her husband following the downing of his plane on April 6, 1994.

The latest court decision means that the case will return to the investigating magistrate for further examination and collection of additional evidence related to Kanziga’s alleged role during the events leading up to and during the genocide.

Richard Gisagara, one of the lawyers representing victims in the case, explained that the Court of Appeal instructed the investigating judge to reopen inquiries and deepen the investigation before determining whether the case should proceed to trial.

“The file has been sent back to the investigating judge to continue gathering evidence concerning her possible role in the Genocide against the Tutsi. Once the investigation is completed, the judge will decide whether there are grounds for trial,” he said.

Agathe Kanziga left Rwanda on April 9, 1994, after being evacuated to France under a decree issued during the presidency of François Mitterrand.

Previous investigations into her alleged role had mainly focused on the first three days following the outbreak of the genocide. However, in September 2024, French prosecutors argued that the inquiry had been too limited in scope, conducted over a short period and based on testimony from only a small number of witnesses.

Prosecutors later requested broader investigations covering the period between March 1 and April 9, 1994, including scrutiny of Kanziga’s alleged involvement in planning activities connected to the genocide.

Kisangani, May 16, 2026 - A military court in the Democratic Republic of Congo has sentenced 58 soldiers to three years in prison after convicting them of disobeying military orders during operations against the Alliance Fleuve Congo/March 23 Movement (AFC/M23) in eastern Congo.

The ruling was delivered by the Military Court sitting in Kisangani, Tshopo Province, following the trial of 84 soldiers arrested in Pinga, a locality in Walikale Territory, North Kivu Province.

The soldiers were accused of abandoning the battlefield in February 2026 and refusing to continue combat operations unless they received unpaid salaries, allowances and food supplies.

According to military prosecutors, some of the soldiers also fired shots into the air during the protest, actions the prosecution argued amounted to mutiny and posed a threat to national security.

Defense lawyer Patience Yengonane told the court that the soldiers’ actions were linked to poor conditions and failures by the government to meet their needs while deployed on the front lines.

On May 15, the court convicted 58 soldiers of violating military orders and sentenced them to three years in prison, while acquitting 16 others due to insufficient evidence.

The judges also ordered further investigations into 10 additional soldiers accused of abandoning their weapons during the incident. Their cases are expected to return to court after a review by military prosecutors.

The prosecution had initially requested the death penalty for all defendants, arguing that the offenses were extremely serious because they undermined military discipline and security operations against AFC/M23.

KIGALI, May 25, 2026 - Rwanda is intensifying efforts to strengthen alternative dispute resolution mechanisms, with senior judicial officials emphasizing that justice should focus not only on punishment but also on reconciliation, social harmony and community healing.

Speaking at a justice sector meeting on May 22, Supreme Court Judge Aloysie Cyanzayire said the country's growing reliance on non-judicial dispute resolution reflects a broader vision of justice aimed at restoring relationships and preserving social cohesion.

“Justice is not only about punishment,” Cyanzayire told participants. “It is also about reconciling relationships, uniting families and safeguarding human dignity.”

The meeting brought together justice sector leaders to assess progress and explore ways to further strengthen mediation, plea bargaining and other alternatives to traditional court proceedings.

According to officials, Rwanda’s alternative dispute resolution program, launched in 2022, has produced significant results. More than 34,000 criminal cases have been settled through plea bargaining since its introduction, while 1,335 criminal cases were resolved through mediation during 2026 alone.

Cyanzayire said the positive outcomes demonstrate the need to expand the initiative, expressing hope that in the future only disputes that cannot be resolved through alternative means will proceed to court.

Judicial authorities report that the program has contributed to a decline in crime in rural communities, where crime rates fell by 24.4 percent during the 2024/2025 fiscal year. The initiative has also helped reduce court backlogs, which declined from 62 percent in 2022 to 49 percent in 2025.

To further support the policy, the Institute of Legal Practice and Development (ILPD) has launched a nationwide training program on plea bargaining and victim-offender mediation. Running from May to July 2026, the program targets judges, prosecutors, investigators and lawyers.

The preliminary decision to open the trial was signed on May 29 by the Chief Registrar of the Kinshasa Military Court, Col Jeanne Françoise Ngalula Mpiana.

Among those also facing trial are several high-ranking officers, including Gen John Numbi Banza Ntambo, who is reported to have fled to Zimbabwe, as well as Gen Maj Maurice Nyembo Kufi, former chief of staff to Gen Tshiwewe. Other accused officers include Brig Gen Chinyabuuma Kamukinde, Brig Gen John Ngoy wa Kabila, and Brig Gen John Sangwa Muhemedi.

The case also involves three colonels and a civilian defendant, bringing the total number of accused to multiple senior military and security figures.

Authorities say the trial is expected to be one of the most significant military proceedings in recent years and may be held partially behind closed doors due to the sensitivity of national security-related evidence.

The defendants face charges including conspiracy, treason, support for terrorist activities, insubordination, desertion, illegal possession of weapons and ammunition, and incitement of military personnel to disobey orders.

Gen Tshiwewe, who served as Commander-in-Chief of the armed forces from 2022 to 2024, was arrested in July 2025 while serving as a military advisor to President Félix Tshisekedi.

At the time of his arrest, authorities did not publicly disclose details, although political figures later alleged he had been involved in a plot against the head of state.

excerpt_en: Arusha, June 8, 2026 - The African Court on Human and Peoples’ Rights has called on Tanzania to remove the mandatory death penalty from its Penal Code, ruling that the current legal framework violates international human rights standards.
body_en:
Arusha, June 8, 2026 - The African Court on Human and Peoples’ Rights has called on Tanzania to remove the mandatory death penalty from its Penal Code, ruling that the current legal framework violates international human rights standards.

The court’s ruling, issued on June 5, 2026, challenges Article 197 of Tanzania’s Penal Code, which prescribes death by hanging as the sole sentence for individuals convicted of murder.

According to the court, the absence of judicial discretion in sentencing undermines fundamental legal principles and infringes on the right to life, as protected under international human rights treaties to which Tanzania is a signatory.

The three-judge panel, presided over by Judge Blaise Tchikaya, concluded that mandatory capital punishment is incompatible with evolving human rights standards, and urged Tanzanian authorities to abolish the practice or amend the law to allow alternative sentencing options.

The case was brought before the court by three death row inmates who argued that their convictions violated their rights to life, dignity, and access to fair legal representation.

In its judgment, the court emphasized that sentencing frameworks must allow judges to consider individual circumstances rather than imposing a uniform punishment for all cases of murder.

The ruling has reignited debate over the use of capital punishment in Tanzania, where the death penalty remains legally in force but is rarely carried out in practice.

Human rights advocates argue that the decision could mark a significant step toward broader abolition efforts across the region, while legal analysts note that implementation will depend on legislative reforms by Tanzanian authorities.

excerpt: PARIS, June 26, 2026 - Dr. Sosthène Munyemana, who is serving a prison sentence in France after being convicted of genocide-related crimes, has refused to testify in the appeal trial of Dr. Eugène Rwamucyo before the Paris Court of Appeal.
title_en: Convicted Genocide Offender Declines to Testify in Dr. Rwamucyo Appeal Trial
excerpt_en: PARIS, June 26, 2026 - Dr. Sosthène Munyemana, who is serving a prison sentence in France after being convicted of genocide-related crimes, has refused to testify in the appeal trial of Dr. Eugène Rwamucyo before the Paris Court of Appeal.
body_en:
PARIS, June 26, 2026 - Dr. Sosthène Munyemana, who is serving a prison sentence in France after being convicted of genocide-related crimes, has refused to testify in the appeal trial of Dr. Eugène Rwamucyo before the Paris Court of Appeal.

Munyemana had also declined to testify during Rwamucyo's initial trial in late 2024, arguing that both men were accused of crimes committed in the same area of Butare during the 1994 Genocide against the Tutsi.

Following the conclusion of his own appeal case in 2025, in which his 24-year prison sentence was upheld, French prosecutors again invited Munyemana to testify in the Rwamucyo proceedings.

Representatives of civil parties said prosecutors requested that Munyemana appear before the court to formally state his position after he declined the invitation.

Appearing before the court on June 24, the 70-year-old reiterated that he would not testify.

"I want to say first of all that I refuse to testify. I will not take the oath, and I do not wish to testify," he told the court.

Neither the prosecution nor lawyers representing victims challenged his decision during the hearing. However, one of Dr. Rwamucyo's defense lawyers, Me Siari Michèle, argued that Munyemana's refusal to testify was problematic for the proceedings.

Dr. Rwamucyo, 67, formerly headed the Center for University Public Health (CUSP) in Butare. He is accused of participating in meetings that allegedly planned the killing of Tutsis during the 1994 Genocide against the Tutsi, overseeing the burial of victims, and ordering attacks on wounded survivors.

Local leaders said the illicit trade remains widespread, with producers increasingly using concealed structures to avoid detection.

The acting Mayor of Kayonza District, Fred Hategekimana, urged residents to cooperate with security agencies by reporting suspected illegal alcohol production and drug-related activities.

According to a statement from the prosecution office, the attorney general stressed the importance of concluding investigations into abuses committed against civilians in conflict zones in order to bring perpetrators to justice.

The committee reviewed operational progress, periodic reports, and mechanisms aimed at improving efficiency following the transfer of its headquarters to Khartoum.

Abdel Aal also emphasized the need to speed up the implementation of the committee’s programs to achieve its objectives, with prosecutors highlighting ongoing efforts to document violations and combat impunity.

Authorities said approximately 12,400 criminal complaints have so far been registered against members of the Rapid Support Forces (RSF). Several RSF leaders, among them commander Mohamed Hamdan Daglo and his brothers Abdel Rahim and Al-Qoni Daglo, are currently facing trial in absentia on charges related to waging war against the state, undermining the constitutional order, and committing war crimes.

Before his defection, Al-Safna held a senior operational role within the RSF, including command responsibilities in North Darfur and participation in offensives that expanded the group’s control in West Kordofan.

The letter claims that approximately 20,000 detainees are being held at a prison facility in Nyala, South Darfur, while additional detainees, including children, are reportedly held at another facility in El Fasher, North Darfur.

According to the document, conditions inside the detention centres have deteriorated sharply, with reports of severe food shortages, disease outbreaks, and rising mortality among inmates.

The Sudanese government also accuses the RSF of extrajudicial killings and the concealment of detainee deaths, as well as the execution of wounded individuals at medical facilities in North Darfur.

The RSF has not publicly responded to the allegations.

Sudan has called for urgent international intervention, including independent investigations and immediate access for humanitarian and monitoring organizations to the detention sites, citing concerns over grave human rights violations.

Kampala, May 21, 2026 - Police in Kampala have arrested four suspects over allegations of defrauding a South African national of USD 103,050 (approximately Shs388.9 million) in a suspected gold scam linked to a fake export transaction.

Investigators say the complainant was promised the sale and export of gold to Dubai, but was instead subjected to repeated payment demands allegedly covering insurance, taxes, and logistics fees.

“The complainant reportedly made payments to facilitate insurance, tax, and logistics costs. However, the promised shipment was never made, and additional demands for money raised suspicion, prompting him to report the matter to police,” Owoyesigyire said.

Following the complaint, security agencies conducted a search at the company premises, where they recovered suspected gold bars and nuggets, a motor vehicle, passports, identification documents, a precious metals analyser, and assorted paperwork believed to be linked to the operation.

Police confirmed the arrest of four suspects identified as Edson Ogwang, Ronald Safari, Joseph Karumba, and Jacob Opio, who are currently assisting with ongoing investigations.

Samples of the suspected precious metals have been submitted to the Government Analytical Laboratory in Entebbe for verification to determine their authenticity.

Authorities also said they have engaged the Uganda Registration Services Bureau (URSB) and the Ministry of Energy and Mineral Development to verify the company’s registration and licensing status.

excerpt: KASESE, June 19, 2026 - The High Court in Kasese has acquitted six individuals facing murder charges in two separate criminal cases, ruling that prosecutors failed to present sufficient evidence to secure convictions.
title_en: Kasese High Court Acquits Six Accused in Separate Murder Trials
excerpt_en: KASESE, June 19, 2026 - The High Court in Kasese has acquitted six individuals facing murder charges in two separate criminal cases, ruling that prosecutors failed to present sufficient evidence to secure convictions.
body_en:
KASESE, June 19, 2026 - The High Court in Kasese has acquitted six individuals facing murder charges in two separate criminal cases, ruling that prosecutors failed to present sufficient evidence to secure convictions.

In the first case, five men charged with murder and aggravated robbery over the killing of Gerald Bwambale, the LCII chairperson of Kyogha Parish, were found not guilty after the court concluded that the prosecution had failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt.

The acquitted men - Allan Bwambale, Timona Muhindo, Obed Muhindo, Noel Masereka, and Joackim Bwambale - had been arrested following the fatal shooting of Bwambale on the night of June 3, 2025. Prosecutors alleged that the local leader was shot while asleep at his home in Bwera Sub-county, Kasese District.

In its judgment, the court found that the prosecution's case relied primarily on circumstantial evidence and failed to directly connect any of the accused to the killing. The court also identified significant weaknesses in the handling of key exhibits, including an alleged firearm, spent cartridges, and projectiles recovered during the investigation.

The court determined that the inconsistencies surrounding the evidence created reasonable doubt, preventing a lawful conviction and resulting in the acquittal of all five defendants.

In a separate judgment delivered the same day, the court also acquitted Brighton Akandwanaho, 20, who had been charged with the murder of Eliphaz Kambale.

Akandwanaho was accused of fatally stabbing Kambale during an altercation at Vegas Bar and Lodge in Majengo Trading Centre on the night of December 24, 2024.

After reviewing the evidence, the court found that testimony presented by key prosecution witnesses contained material contradictions and failed to establish the accused's guilt beyond reasonable doubt.

excerpt_en: WAKISO, June 22, 2026 - Police have rescued 18 children from a house in Wakiso District and arrested two suspects as part of an investigation into a suspected human trafficking operation.
body_en:
WAKISO, June 22, 2026 - Police have rescued 18 children from a house in Wakiso District and arrested two suspects as part of an investigation into a suspected human trafficking operation.

The operation was conducted on June 21 at a residence in Kakunyu Village, Wakiso Town Council, after local authorities reported that an unusually large number of children were being housed at the premises.

During the raid, officers found 18 children-nine boys and nine girls-aged between three and 12 years living in two rooms under circumstances investigators considered suspicious.

Preliminary investigations indicate that the children had allegedly been transported from Luweero and Masindi districts, although the purpose and circumstances of their relocation remain under investigation.

Police arrested two suspects identified as George Mulindwa (33), a teacher, and Madinah Babirye (24), a casual worker. They remain in custody as detectives investigate possible human trafficking and related offenses.

The rescued children have been placed under protective care while authorities work to establish their identities and reunite them with their parents or guardians. The identification process is being conducted in collaboration with child protection and social welfare agencies.

Investigators are also seeking to determine whether the case is linked to a broader child trafficking network operating across multiple districts.

Authorities have urged parents and guardians whose children may have disappeared under suspicious circumstances to report the cases to the nearest police station as investigations continue. They also warned the public against participating in or facilitating child trafficking and called on communities to remain vigilant and report suspected cases promptly.

body_en:
Kampala, June 3, 2026 - The High Court in Kampala has temporarily halted the implementation of a decision by the Insurance Regulatory Authority (IRA) Board declining to recommend Chief Executive Officer Ibrahim Lubega Kaddunabbi for contract renewal, pending the determination of a judicial review application challenging the process.

The interim administrative order, issued by Justice Joyce Kavuma on May 29, preserves the status quo while the court considers a substantive application filed by Kaddunabbi contesting the legality of the board’s February 16, 2026 decision.

The ruling bars the IRA Board from implementing, enforcing, or acting upon its decision not to recommend Kaddunabbi for reappointment until the court reaches a final determination on the matter.

At the centre of the dispute is Kaddunabbi’s argument that the process leading to the board’s decision was procedurally flawed and should be subjected to judicial review. Through his legal team, he maintains that he retains rights arising from his employment contract that warrant protection while the case is being heard.

The Insurance Regulatory Authority and its board chairperson, Dr Isaac Nabeta Nkoote, opposed the request for interim relief, arguing that Kaddunabbi’s contract was nearing expiry and that preserving his position through a court order would effectively amount to extending or renewing his contract, a mandate they contend falls within the authority of appointing bodies under the law.

Despite the court order, the ruling does not automatically reinstate Kaddunabbi as chief executive. On June 1, the IRA Board appointed Protazio Sande, the regulator’s Director of Strategy and Market Development, to serve as acting Chief Executive Officer pending further developments.
